lessonTitle: Pancreatitis and Biliary Disease: Diagnosis, Severity and Drainage

blocks.text: After a weekend of heavy drinking, a 49-year-old man arrives doubled over with epigastric pain that bores straight through to his back. He is vomiting, tachycardic and cannot lie flat; he is more comfortable leaning forward. A single blood test will confirm what you suspect, but how you judge severity in the next 48 hours will determine whether he needs a ward bed or intensive care.

blocks.markdown: **Acute pancreatitis** is inflammation of the pancreas caused by premature intrapancreatic activation of digestive enzymes (trypsinogen to trypsin), leading to autodigestion, local oedema or necrosis and a systemic inflammatory response. The two commonest causes are **gallstones** (a stone obstructing the ampulla of Vater or passing through it) and **alcohol**. Other causes: hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, post-ERCP, drugs, trauma, autoimmune disease, viral infection, and idiopathic cases (a mnemonic such as GET SMASHED lists them).

blocks.title: Diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis
blocks.text: Diagnosis requires at least two of three: (1) characteristic abdominal pain (acute epigastric, often radiating to the back); (2) serum amylase or lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal (ULN); (3) characteristic imaging (CT, MRI or ultrasound). Lipase is preferred because it is more specific and remains elevated longer than amylase; reference ranges vary by laboratory.

blocks.title: Applying the diagnostic criteria
blocks.prompt: A 33-year-old woman has 12 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Her serum lipase is 540 U/L (laboratory ULN 60 U/L). Does she meet the diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis?

steps.text: Criterion 2: express the lipase as a multiple of the ULN.
9 times ULN is greater than 3 times ULN, so criterion 2 is met.
Two of three criteria are met, so imaging is not required to make the diagnosis, though ultrasound is still needed to look for gallstones.

blocks.answer: Yes: acute pancreatitis is diagnosed on pain plus lipase 9 times the upper limit of normal; ultrasound then seeks a gallstone cause.

blocks.markdown: **Assessing severity.** Within 48 hours, a multifactorial score such as the **Glasgow-Imrie (modified Glasgow) score** is used: one point each for PaO2 below 8 kPa, age above 55 years, neutrophil (white cell) count above 15 x 10^9/L, calcium below 2.0 mmol/L, urea above 16 mmol/L, LDH above 600 U/L (or AST/ALT above 200 U/L), albumin below 32 g/L and glucose above 10 mmol/L (no known diabetes). A score of 3 or more predicts severe disease. The revised Atlanta classification grades mild (no organ failure), moderately severe (transient organ failure under 48 hours or local complications) and severe (persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours). A CRP above about 150 mg/L at 48 hours also signals severity.

blocks.title: Scoring severity by Glasgow-Imrie
blocks.prompt: A 44-year-old man with pancreatitis has PaO2 7.6 kPa, white cell count 12 x 10^9/L, calcium 1.92 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, LDH 640 U/L, albumin 35 g/L and glucose 7 mmol/L. Calculate his score.

steps.text: Age 44 is not above 55: 0. White cells 12 do not exceed 15: 0.
PaO2 7.6 is below 8: 1 point. Calcium 1.92 is below 2.0: 1 point.
Urea 8 is not above 16: 0. LDH 640 exceeds 600: 1 point.
Albumin 35 is not below 32: 0. Glucose 7 does not exceed 10: 0.

blocks.answer: Score 3, which predicts severe pancreatitis and should prompt senior review and consideration of critical care.

blocks.caption: Supportive care in acute pancreatitis
rows: Early intravenous crystalloid with frequent reassessment; avoid over-resuscitation
Regular multimodal analgesia, opioids as needed
Oxygen to maintain saturation; track urine output, observations, organ function
Early oral or enteral feeding as tolerated rather than prolonged fasting
Not routinely given for prophylaxis; reserved for proven infection (e.g. infected necrosis, cholangitis)
Gallstones: ERCP if cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild disease; stop alcohol; treat triglycerides or calcium

blocks.markdown: **Obstructive jaundice** results from impaired bile flow: pale stools, dark urine, itching and a cholestatic liver profile (rise in alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia). Causes include common bile duct stones, pancreatic head carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, strictures and external compression. *Painless* jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder suggests malignant obstruction (Courvoisier's sign). First-line imaging is ultrasound to look for duct dilatation (common bile duct above 6 mm) and stones; MRCP defines the biliary tree non-invasively; ERCP allows therapeutic stone removal, sphincterotomy and stenting; EUS characterises ampullary and pancreatic lesions.

blocks.title: Ascending cholangitis is a surgical emergency
blocks.text: Infected, obstructed bile causes Charcot's triad of fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain; Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and confusion and indicates severe sepsis. Treatment is resuscitation, blood cultures, early intravenous antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage, usually by ERCP with stenting or stone removal (percutaneous or surgical drainage if ERCP fails). Antibiotics alone are not sufficient.

items: Pancreatitis: pain, lipase above 3 times ULN, check cause with ultrasound, calcium and triglycerides.
Severity: Glasgow-Imrie within 48 hours, CRP at 48 hours, organ support if failing.
Obstructive jaundice: LFT pattern, ultrasound, then MRCP or ERCP.
Cholangitis: resuscitate, antibiotics, then urgent drainage.

blocks.title: Amylase versus lipase
blocks.text: Amylase rises within hours and falls within days, and is also raised in other conditions (parotitis, bowel perforation). Lipase stays elevated for longer and is more specific, so it is preferred where available. Neither level correlates with severity.

points: Acute pancreatitis needs two of: typical pain, lipase or amylase above 3 times ULN, characteristic imaging; gallstones and alcohol are the commonest causes.
Severity is judged by Glasgow-Imrie (score 3 or more is severe), CRP at 48 hours and organ failure; the enzyme level does not predict severity.
Supportive care is fluids, analgesia, oxygen, early feeding, with no routine prophylactic antibiotics.
Obstructive jaundice is investigated with ultrasound then MRCP or ERCP; cholangitis requires resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage.

questions.stem: Which blood test is generally preferred to confirm acute pancreatitis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lipase is specific and stays elevated for longer than amylase.
distractorRationale.c: Troponin tests for myocardial injury, though it helps exclude an MI mimic.
distractorRationale.d: Ferritin is an acute-phase and iron-storage marker, not diagnostic for pancreatitis.

questions.explanation: Lipase is more specific than amylase and remains raised for longer, making it the preferred diagnostic enzyme. A level above three times the upper limit of normal supports the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has typical epigastric pain radiating to the back. Her serum lipase is 1.8 times the ULN, but CT shows pancreatic oedema and peripancreatic fluid. Does she meet the diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis?

options.text: Yes, because typical pain and characteristic imaging are two of the three criteria
No, because lipase must exceed three times ULN in every case
No, because the diagnosis needs surgery
Only if amylase is also raised

questions.correctOptionText: Yes, because typical pain and characteristic imaging are two of the three criteria

distractorRationale.a: Correct: any two of pain, enzymes above 3 times ULN and imaging suffice.
distractorRationale.b: Enzymes are only one of three criteria.
distractorRationale.d: A second enzyme is not required.

questions.explanation: The diagnosis needs any two of three criteria, so typical pain plus characteristic imaging is sufficient even when enzymes are below the threshold. A modestly raised lipase may reflect late presentation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has 3 weeks of painless progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and weight loss. The gallbladder is palpable and non-tender. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas

questions.correctOptionText: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas

distractorRationale.a: Correct: painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignant obstruction (Courvoisier's sign).
distractorRationale.b: A stone typically causes pain and a shrunken, fibrosed gallbladder.
distractorRationale.c: Viral hepatitis does not cause pale stools with a palpable gallbladder.
distractorRationale.d: Haemolysis causes unconjugated jaundice with normal stools and urine bilirubin absent.

questions.explanation: Courvoisier's law states that a palpable gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to gallstones, because chronic stone disease scars the gallbladder. A dilated, distensible gallbladder points to a malignant obstruction downstream such as a pancreatic head tumour.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has fever, rigors, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, blood pressure 86/50 mmHg and new confusion. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Resuscitation, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage by ERCP

questions.correctOptionText: Resuscitation, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage by ERCP

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is severe cholangitis (Reynolds' pentad) needing source control.
distractorRationale.c: Elective surgery does not treat acute obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: Antibiotics alone fail without drainage of the obstructed system.

questions.explanation: Fever, jaundice, pain, hypotension and confusion is Reynolds' pentad, indicating severe cholangitis. Obstructed infected bile must be drained urgently, while sepsis is treated with fluids and antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with mild acute pancreatitis is haemodynamically stable. Which supportive measure is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, analgesia and early oral feeding as tolerated, without routine antibiotics
Strict nil by mouth for a week

questions.correctOptionText: Intravenous crystalloid, analgesia and early oral feeding as tolerated, without routine antibiotics

distractorRationale.a: Correct: supportive care with early feeding.
distractorRationale.b: Prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely recommended.
distractorRationale.c: Prolonged fasting is outdated; early feeding reduces complications.
distractorRationale.d: Necrosectomy is for infected necrosis, not mild disease.

questions.explanation: Mild pancreatitis is managed with fluids, analgesia and early feeding while the cause is sought. Antibiotics are reserved for proven infection.

questions.stem: The height of the serum amylase or lipase reliably predicts the severity of acute pancreatitis.
questions.explanation: Enzyme levels help diagnosis but do not correlate with severity. Severity is judged by organ failure and scores such as Glasgow-Imrie.

questions.stem: A patient with severe epigastric pain has a serum lipase of 1,050 U/L; the laboratory upper limit of normal is 70 U/L. By what multiple of the upper limit of normal is the lipase raised? (give the multiple to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: The multiple is 1050 / 70 = 15. This exceeds the diagnostic threshold of three times the ULN, so the biochemical criterion is met.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old patient with pancreatitis has: PaO2 9.4 kPa, white cell count 16.5 x 10^9/L, calcium 2.05 mmol/L, urea 17.2 mmol/L, LDH 580 U/L, albumin 29 g/L and glucose 11.4 mmol/L (not diabetic). Using the Glasgow-Imrie criteria in the lesson, calculate the score (points).
questions.explanation: Age above 55 scores 1, white cell count above 15 scores 1, urea above 16 scores 1, albumin below 32 scores 1 and glucose above 10 scores 1, while PaO2 (above 8), calcium (not below 2.0) and LDH (not above 600) score 0. The total is 5, indicating severe pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman presents with jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. Describe how you would confirm that the jaundice is obstructive and how you would investigate the cause.
markingGuide: Features of cholestasis: pale stools, dark urine, pruritus
Cholestatic LFT pattern: raised ALP and GGT with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Ultrasound first: duct dilatation (CBD above 6 mm), gallstones, masses
MRCP to define the biliary tree and cause
ERCP for therapeutic stone clearance or stenting; EUS or CT for pancreatic mass
Painless jaundice and palpable gallbladder suggests malignancy; fever and pain suggest stones or cholangitis
questions.explanation: Obstruction is recognised by the clinical triad of pale stools, dark urine and itching and a cholestatic liver profile. Imaging then identifies level and cause, escalating from ultrasound to MRCP, then ERCP for treatment.

questions.stem: Explain how severity of acute pancreatitis is assessed in the first 48 hours and outline the principles of supportive care and when ERCP is indicated.
markingGuide: Glasgow-Imrie criteria within 48 hours, score 3 or more is severe
Revised Atlanta: mild, moderately severe, severe (persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours)
CRP at 48 hours above about 150 mg/L indicates severity
Early intravenous fluids with reassessment, oxygen, analgesia, urine output monitoring
ERCP for gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction
Critical care for organ failure; cholecystectomy in same admission for mild gallstone disease
questions.explanation: Severity guides the level of care because organ failure drives mortality, not enzyme levels. Care is supportive, with ERCP reserved for biliary obstruction or infection.
